cells.tense: You are the one who can hear the shape of the argument before it lands.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin one small new thing with your group before its point is clear — a standing dinner, a question worth asking. Let it stay unproven for now.
cells.core:
Around a table where a shared story gets kept alive, you hear what the story is doing. Someone says the old phrase almost by shape and you can see where it leads, so you name the move before it lands and the others follow the idea the way they follow a road they know. That is the clean half of your accuracy. It holds because you have heard the pattern enough times, not because you are guessing it.

The open end here is making something, not only naming things. Begin once before it is legible. Pick a small new thing and do it without being able to show what it will become. What matters is not the thing you begin. It is that the people you sit with get a first move they did not have before, and you find out what is on the other side of starting.

cells.tense: You are already three steps into the argument your group has not had yet.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Choose the thing your group keeps circling and carry it through this month — call the gathering, write the message, whatever moves it past where it is stuck.
cells.core:
You have moved past listening to what the group's story is doing and started seeing three moves ahead of it. Gatherings pause because you have already priced the outcome; a half-finished sentence gets you there first. You have the pattern right and you are four beats in front of the table, which turns a good map into a forecast no one agreed to stand under.

The correction is not less thinking. A pattern only frees a group when the group can stand on it, so the repair is one act that cares about the shape it makes. Settle the argument being rehearsed, say the thing plainly, hold the gathering being walked around. One act, chosen with the shape of these people in mind, puts your call back on the table where they sit.

cells.tense: You have stood at the edge of the group's talk so long you are still standing where you used to read it.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: Take one old story the group keeps and pass it on by making it with someone — cook the dish together, walk the route — as often as it takes for them to carry it alone.
cells.core:
Where the group keeps its old stories, you are no longer taking your turn telling them. You can still see exactly where the phrase lands; you just do not reach for it, and that listening has gone quiet. It does not vanish, it goes unwalked, and a group carries its pattern in the talking and the making, not in one person's reading.

Empty seats do not fill by effort. They fill by where a person puts their hands. Hand one old thing to one person and do it with them until they can do it without you — the dish, the route, the story that needs a voice. That is teaching, and it is also connection, and doing it changes the teller back before it changes the group.

cells.tense: You are already reading the group's story and calling it nothing.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: When you catch yourself reading a conversation for someone, ask how it actually feels to them. Then wait — let their answer sit there with you, however long that takes.
cells.core:
Something in you catches the shape of what a group is saying and says what it finds before you have decided to speak. Most people do not notice, but the person beside you does, and you have been saying it is just your mouth. That is also why people bring you things they cannot say elsewhere, though you cannot say why.

Behind the speed, the simpler act is sitting. When someone is with you, ask them how it actually feels and do not answer your own question. If the exchange gets hard, stay in it until you can hear them. That is compassion as a behavior, and it arrives before the words. Reclaiming the thinking starts here.
cells.sheetLine: Your mouth runs the read before your mind has caught on.
